purpose: Fosinopril is used to treat high blood pressure (hypertension) and heart failure. Lowering your blood pressure helps reduce your risk of having a stroke, heart attack, or kidney problems. Your doctor may also prescribe it to protect your kidneys if you have diabetes.
how_it_works: Your body makes a chemical called angiotensin II that tightens your blood vessels and raises your blood pressure. Fosinopril blocks the enzyme your body uses to make that chemical. This helps your blood vessels relax and open up, making it easier for your heart to pump blood and lowering your blood pressure.
common_side_effects: The most common side effect is a dry, nagging cough that does not go away — this happens in some people and is the main reason patients switch medications. You might also feel dizzy, especially when you stand up quickly. Other possible side effects include headache, fatigue, nausea, and mild skin rash.
warnings: Do NOT take fosinopril if you are pregnant or planning to become pregnant, as it can cause serious harm or death to an unborn baby. Tell your doctor if you have ever had a severe allergic reaction with swelling of your face, lips, tongue, or throat (called angioedema), because fosinopril can cause this too. Avoid potassium supplements or salt substitutes containing potassium unless your doctor approves, as this medicine can raise potassium levels in your blood. Be careful if you also take NSAIDs like ibuprofen or naproxen, as they can reduce how well fosinopril works and harm your kidneys.
typical_dosing: For high blood pressure, the usual starting dose is 10 mg once a day. Your doctor may increase it up to 40 mg once a day depending on how your blood pressure responds. For heart failure, dosing starts lower and is adjusted carefully by your doctor. Take it at the same time each day, with or without food.
